https://www.dw.com/en/ceuta-spain-sets-u.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ISwS Nearly all of the people who rushed Ceuta's border have since left, but those who do stay are unlikely to be able to reach the European mainland unless they are formally granted permission to reside [FILE: August 6, 2026] Image: Violeta Santos Moura/REUTERS Advertisement Spain 's government on Friday moved to impose reciprocal entry checks on people traveling from Italy . The Spanish government had warned that it would do so unless Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni 's governemnt lifted the border measures it has implemented against Spain. Italy's right-wing government announced the checks at the height of the social media panic as tens of thousands of people gained entry to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco last week. The checks are essentially symbolic, given that Ceuta is not on the European mainland and Italy and Spain do not share a land border, meaning that the vast majority of people potentially affected are tourists on planes. Nevertheless, the issue has turned into a point of dispute between two governments of different ideological persuasions with contrasting messaging priorities on migration policy. Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did Spain say about checks on travelers from Italy? The border controls on Italy will go into effect from midnight ‌on ⁠Saturday ⁠until September 7, the Spanish government said. Border agents will check passport, nationality and visas for Italian passengers and visitors from other ​countries arriving from Italy. Spain had called Italy's decision to impose checks on people arriving from Spain "unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against ​the Spanish population." Madrid said there was no real risk of people who overwhelmed Ceuta's border controls reaching the European mainland, let alone Italy. It pointed to the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 people returning to Morocco within days . Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also drew attention to the higher numbers of irregular migrants reaching Italian than Spanish territory in recent years. "If [Italy] fails to [remove the entry checks] before Sunday, August 9, Spain will be forced to adopt proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens," the government said. Italy replied later Friday that it would not accept "ultimatums ⁠or ⁠impositions" from Madrid, and that it would maintain the suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15. Despite Spain's objections, an array of European countries, including Germany, and the European Commission all made comments about the importance of border security to the open-border Schengen Zone amid the public uproar. Italy was among comparatively few to go so far as to frame the issue as "suspending" Spain's Schengen status, however. Italy first made the announcement as images and footage of the border breach were going viral online Image: Atlas/REUTERS What do we know about Italy's checks on travelers from Spain? Details on precisely what checks, if any, Italy has actually implemented over the past week have been thin on the ground. Migration analyst Gerald Knaus told DW earlier this week that the move was "pure populism" and a "completely bizarre" measure. "They don't have a border, so it's only for a few flights," Knaus said. "It makes no sense in the high tourist season. And as Giorgia Meloni indicated, it shouldn't inconvenience travelers." Knaus said the decision could only be understood in the context of domestic political appearances, not foreign policy realities. "I think to understand it, you must understand that on [Meloni's] right, there is a radical right party in Italy that puts pressure on her. And so politicians everywhere in Europe, when they see these images which create fear, are looking for something to say — something to do that makes them look tough." EU defends border response after Ceuta crossing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Meloni and Sanchez: A clash of styles on migration At least in terms of their stated positions and approaches, Italy and Spain have quite different stances on the issue of migration. Meloni came to power in 2022 in Italy, after several years of much higher irregular migration rates and asylum applications caused in large part by the wars in Syria and Ukraine. She promised a tougher line on migration into one of the most common landing points in southern Europe. Sanchez, meanwhile, has championed a more pro-migration stance during his two terms in office. He argues that Spain's economy needs migration and offered an amnesty and temporary residency permit process earlier this year to irregular migrants already in the country. Sanchez said it was better to grant residency and start collecting taxes than to keep people out of the formal labor market. Migration expert Knaus, however, warned against overstating the practical differences between the two countries, saying Meloni faced similar economic requirements and was actually pursuing comparable policies — only with much less public fanfare. "Italy is doing something very similar. Hundreds of thousands of people are brought in or are already in the country and are regularized for the Italian labour market under Giorgia Meloni," Knaus said. "And 1.6 million people were regularized under various Italian governments in the last 20 years." Don't let the algorithm hide the news. In this festival organized by Texapoker , players from all around Europe didn't miss the opportunity to try to add a piece of jewelry to their collection. But after three days of play, the most coveted ring, the €1,500 WSOP Circuit Main Event ring, now belongs to Luca Topazio . From a field of 879 entries , which generated a total prize pool of €1,115,451 , he used his aggressive style of play to win the €200,000 first-place prize , as well as a €5,000 package for the next WSOP Paradise. During the final table, he battled especially hard against Radoslaw Kopec , who finished runner-up once again after already taking second place in the WSOP Circuit Middelkerke Main Event last year. 2026 WSOP Circuit Malta Main Event final table results Place Player Country Prize 1 Luca Topazio Italy €200,000 2 Radoslaw Kopec Poland €125,000 3 Lucas van den Belt Netherlands €85,000 4 Matteo Ricco Italy €60,000 5 Aleksandar Georgiev Bulgaria €43,000 6 Alberto Cigliano Italy €31,000 7 Vitali Bibik Poland €23,000 8 Christoffer Jensen Denmark €17,300 9 Nicola Bordignon Italy €14,191 Winner's reaction Sixteen years ago, Luca Topazio started his poker career with a €190,000 cash thanks to his victory in an Italian Poker Tour Main Event. This result remained his biggest score... until today. "I am very happy, I played a very good poker," translated a tournament director from Topazio's Italian. But even though the two results look quite similar in terms of prize money, the experience he gained in the years between them helped him go even further this time. "I am more mature now. I adapted my game to get this result," he added. His game, judging from what he showed at the table, looked loose, but he was not afraid to attack at all. "My strategy as the chip leader was to make everyone short and to kill everyone," explained the professional poker player. This approach brought him the title today, as well as other strong results such as an 11th-place finish in the last EPT Barcelona Mystery Bounty. Based on this success, Topazio now plans to play the Battle of Malta here at Casino Malta at the end of the month, followed by EPT Prague in December. And, of course, he will head to the Bahamas for WSOP Paradise, where he will try to take today's success to another level. WSOP Circuit Malta Final Table Action With no player under 20 big blinds at the beginning of the final table, all nine finalists knew they had to be patient, but it didn't take long to see Christoffer Jensen being the first one to go all-in and double with queens through Aleksandar Georgiev 's ace-king. A few hands later, Nicola Bordignon wasn't as lucky with fives and became the first player to be eliminated. Now down to eight players, the live stream started, but Jensen eventually played another coin flip to survive. He didn't make it this time against Lucas van den Belt and took €17,300 for his eighth-place finish. At the same time, Vitali Bibik managed to double up , and so did Georgiev thanks to a lucky runner-runner flush . They both remained the two shortest stacks, however, by the next break, after which Bibik was at risk again with queen-ten . Matteo Ricco had ace-seven and held to send the Polish player to the rail (7th - €23,000), then doubled up through Kopec . Alberto Cigliano was hoping to double as well with king-queen, but ran into Van den Belt's aces to finish in sixth place (€31,000). Georgiev (5th - €43,000) suffered the same fate ten minutes later against eventual winner Topazio. Luca Topazio Radislaw Kopec On top of the counts, Kopec was one card away from elimination but hit an ace on the river to double up and take the chip lead back. The same went for Topazio with ace-queen over ace-jack before Van den Belt bluffed him to make him fold aces and level up the stacks of the four remaining players. Kopec eventually regained the lead by eliminating Ricco (4th - €60,000), and extended it even after he doubled Van den Belt . This didn't last long, however, as Topazio made a good hero call and then hit a full house . He also took Van den Belt's stack (3rd - €85,000) to start heads-up play with a 5:1 chip lead. With such a big advantage, Topazio needed just two hands to end the tournament, hitting a full house to be crowned the 2026 WSOP Circuit Malta Main Event champion!
